mainTopic: Forcing a spouse to move (town and city, nicer homes, ארץ ישראל and ירושלים), which currency pays a כתובה, and the value of living in ארץ ישראל.
overview: This amud finishes the משנה about when a husband may make his wife move. He may not force a move between a small town (עיר) and a big city (כרך) in either direction. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל adds that she may refuse even a move to a nicer home, because any change of routine is hard on the body, as שמואל taught. A new משנה then rules that either spouse may force the family to move up to ארץ ישראל or to ירושלים, but no one may force them to leave. A ברייתא spells out the price of refusing: a wife loses her כתובה, and a husband must divorce her and pay it. Next the גמרא explains which country's money pays a כתובה. רבה says the first תנא holds a כתובה is דרבנן and so always allows the cheaper money, while רבן שמעון בן גמליאל holds it is דאורייתא. A ברייתא about loan documents is clarified along the way. The amud ends with strong praise for living in ארץ ישראל, and then begins the story of רבי זירא hiding from רב יהודה, who held that leaving בבל breaks a מצות עשה. That story continues on the next amud.

steps.title: No forced move between a town and a big city
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that a husband cannot force his wife to move from an עיר to a כרך, or from a כרך to an עיר.
steps.simpleTranslation: But a husband may not make his wife move from a town to a big city, and not from a big city to a town.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה is finishing its list of moves a husband may and may not force. Even when both places are in the same land, he cannot force a move between a small town and a big city, in either direction.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before this line, the משנה dealt with moving from one land to another. Now it adds a limit on moves within one land. A change in the kind of place you live is a big change in daily life, so the wife can refuse either direction. The גמרא will soon ask why both directions are forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: But not, which sets a limit on the rule before it

steps.confusionAlert: This rule applies even inside the same land. It is not about moving to or from ארץ ישראל.

phrases.english: But not from a town to a big city,
and not from a big city to a town.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the earlier lines of the משנה about forcing a spouse to move between lands.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A husband may not force his wife to move between an עיר and a כרך, in either direction.

steps.title: Moving from a bad home to a nice home
steps.stepSummary: The תנא קמא rules that a husband may move his wife from a bad home to a nice one, but not from a nice home to a bad one.
steps.simpleTranslation: A husband may move his wife from a bad home to a nice home. He may not move her from a nice home to a bad home.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a new rule about the quality of the house. Moving up to a nicer home is allowed, but moving down to a worse home is not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea is simple: a wife cannot reasonably object to an upgrade, but a downgrade harms her. This is the first opinion in the משנה. The next step brings a תנא who disagrees about the upgrade.

keyTerms.meaning: One may take out, meaning one may move her
A home or place to live

phrases.english: One may move her from a bad home to a nice home,
phrases.notes: Some versions have an extra ה in round brackets (הרעה). The corrected wording leaves it out and reads הרע.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל לֹא מִנָּוֶה הַיָּפֶה לְנָוֶה הָרַע(ה).
phrases.english: but not from a nice home to a bad home.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second kind of move, about the quality of the home instead of the type of place.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A husband may force a move up to a nicer home, but not down to a worse one.

steps.title: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל: even an upgrade can be refused
steps.stepSummary: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל holds that a husband cannot force his wife to move even from a bad home to a nice one, because a nice home 'tests' a person.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: he may not even move her from a bad home to a nice home, because a nice home tests a person.
steps.whatsHappening: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל disagrees with the first opinion. He says the wife may refuse even a move to a nicer home.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His reason is that a nice home 'tests' a person. A change of surroundings can be hard on the body, even when the new place is better. So both directions are a change she can refuse, much like the עיר and כרך rule.

keyTerms.meaning: Tests, meaning it puts a strain on a person

steps.confusionAlert: 'A nice home tests' does not mean the nice home is bad. It means that getting used to any new home, even a better one, can be hard on a person.
steps.whatToRemember: The first opinion allows an upgrade but forbids a downgrade. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל forbids forcing a move in either direction, because any change of home is a strain.

phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:

phrases.aramaic: אַף לֹא מִנָּוֶה רַע(ה) לְנָוֶה יָפֶה,
phrases.english: Not even from a bad home to a nice home,
because the nice home tests a person.
phrases.notes: He means the change itself can make a person feel unwell, even when the new place is nicer.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר: אַף לֹא מִנָּוֶה רַע לְנָוֶה יָפֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with the first half of the previous step's ruling.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A wife may refuse even a move from a bad home to a nice home, because a nice home 'tests' a person.

steps.title: Why can't he move her from a town to a big city?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא understands why leaving a כרך for an עיר is a hardship, but asks why moving from an עיר to a כרך is also forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense that he cannot move her from a big city to a town, because a big city has everything and a town does not. But what is the reason he cannot move her from a town to a big city?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the first rule of this section, about עיר and כרך. It explains one direction easily, then asks for the reason behind the other direction.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Leaving a כרך is clearly a loss, because everything is easy to get there and harder to find in a town. Moving to a כרך looks like a gain, so why may she refuse it? The answer comes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: It makes sense, granted. This opens a question that contrasts one easy case with a hard one
All things, everything a person needs

phrases.english: GEMARA: It makes sense that not from a big city to a town,
because in a big city everything is available,
while in a town not everything is available.
But from a town to a big city, what is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the עיר and כרך rule from step 1 and asks for its reason.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why a wife may refuse a move from an עיר to a כרך, when a כרך seems like an improvement.

steps.title: Living in a big city is hard: a proof from נחמיה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the משנה supports רבי יוסי בר חנינא, who learns from a פסוק in נחמיה that living in big cities is hard.
steps.simpleTranslation: This supports רבי יוסי בר חנינא. He said: How do we know that living in big cities is hard? Because it says: 'And the people blessed all the men who offered themselves to live in Jerusalem.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by saying that city life is hard. This matches a teaching of רבי יוסי בר חנינא, which is based on a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In נחמיה, the people gave a blessing to those who agreed to live in ירושלים. You only bless people for taking on something hard, so living in a big city must be a burden. That is why a wife may refuse to move from a quiet town to a כרך.

keyTerms.meaning: It supports him, meaning the משנה backs up this אמורא's view

steps.whatToRemember: A wife can refuse a move in both directions. Leaving a כרך means losing easy access to everything. Moving to a כרך means taking on the hard life of a big city, as the blessing in נחמיה shows.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that halacha treats a wife's lifestyle and comfort as real rights. A husband cannot force big changes in her living conditions on her.

phrases.aramaic: מְסַיַּיע לֵיהּ לְרַבִּי יוֹסֵי בַּר חֲנִינָא.
phrases.english: This supports Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina.
For Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina said:
From where do we know that living in big cities is hard?
As it says: 'And the people blessed'
phrases.notes: נחמיה 11:2

phrases.english: all the men who volunteered
to live in Jerusalem.'

steps.triggerLanguage: מְסַיַּיע לֵיהּ לְרַבִּי יוֹסֵי בַּר חֲנִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 4.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Living in a כרך is itself a hardship, as shown by the people blessing those who volunteered to live in ירושלים. So a wife may refuse to move there.

steps.title: What does 'tests' mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes רבן שמעון בן גמליאל from the משנה and asks what he means when he says a nice home 'tests' a person.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל said a nice home tests a person. What does 'tests' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's words in the משנה and asks what the word 'בודק' means. This sets up the explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: It sounds strange that a wife could refuse to move to a nicer home. The whole ruling depends on what 'tests' means, so the גמרא asks for a definition.

keyTerms.meaning: Tests or checks. Here it means the new place puts a person through a hard test.
'Etc.' The rest of the quote is understood.
What? It asks for the meaning of a word or idea.

phrases.aramaic: רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר כּוּ׳.
phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says, etc.
phrases.notes: This quotes the משנה from Step 3, where he said a nice home 'tests' a person.

phrases.english: What is the meaning of "tests"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the ruling of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל from Step 3 to explain a word in it.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The meaning of 'בודק' in רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's statement.

steps.title: A change in routine can make you sick
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains 'tests' using שמואל's rule that any change in routine is the start of stomach illness.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is like שמואל said: a change in your routine is the beginning of stomach sickness.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that a new home 'tests' a person because, as שמואל taught, any change in routine can make you sick.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point is not whether the new home is better or worse. Any change at all is hard on the body. So the wife may refuse to move even to a nicer home.

keyTerms.meaning: Like שמואל. It follows his opinion.
A change in one's regular routine or habits.

steps.whyThisMatters: This explains the reason behind רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's whole ruling: the change itself is the harm.

phrases.english: It is in line with Shmuel.
As Shmuel said:
A change in one's routine
is the beginning of stomach illness.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 6.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'בודק' means the move tests a person's health, because any change in routine can cause stomach illness.

steps.title: בן סירא: all the days of the poor are bad
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes בן סירא, who says all the days of a poor person are bad.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is written in the book of בן סירא: All the days of a poor man are bad.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a saying from ספר בן סירא that every day of a poor person's life is bad. This sets up the question in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This saying will turn out to rest on the same idea as שמואל's rule. The גמרא brings it here so it can show that link in the next two steps.

keyTerms.meaning: The book of בן סירא, an old book of wise sayings.

phrases.english: It is written in the book of Ben Sira:
"All the days of a poor man are bad."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a related saying that will also be explained by שמואל's rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Every day of a poor person's life is bad.

steps.title: But poor people enjoy שבת and יום טוב
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges בן סירא: a poor person has שבתות and ימים טובים, which are good days.
steps.simpleTranslation: But there are שבתות and ימים טובים!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how בן סירא can say every day of a poor person is bad. On שבת and יום טוב even the poor eat well.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge targets the word 'all'. If even some days are good for the poor, the saying seems too strong.

keyTerms.meaning: 'But there is.' It points out a case that seems to go against the statement.

phrases.english: But there are Shabbatot and Festivals!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the saying quoted in Step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: בן סירא's statement that all the days of the poor are bad.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: On שבת and יום טוב the poor eat well, so not all of their days are bad.

steps.title: Even a good change hurts the poor
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers with שמואל's rule again: the change to rich food on שבת is itself harmful.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is like שמואל said: a change in routine is the beginning of stomach sickness.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that even the nice food of שבת and יום טוב is a change from the poor person's normal diet. That change can make him sick.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same rule of שמואל now does two jobs. It explains why a nicer home can be harmful, and why even good days are hard for a poor person. In both cases a change for the better is still a change.
steps.whatToRemember: שמואל's rule, 'a change in routine is the start of illness', explains both רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's ruling and בן סירא's saying. Even a change for the better can do harm.
steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא repeats שמואל's exact words on purpose. This is not a copying mistake. The same rule is used a second time to answer a new question.

phrases.english: It is in line with Shmuel.
As Shmuel said:
A change in one's routine
is the beginning of stomach illness.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 9.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: שבת and יום טוב are good days for the poor because they eat well.
steps.terutzMaskana: The change to rich food is itself harmful to the poor, so even those days are bad for them.

steps.title: בן סירא: even the poor man's nights are bad
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the rest of בן סירא's words: the poor man's house sits low and his vineyard sits high, so rain floods his roof and washes away his soil.
steps.simpleTranslation: בן סירא says: Even the nights are bad. His roof is the lowest of the roofs, and his vineyard is at the top of the mountains. The rain from the roofs runs onto his roof, and the soil of his vineyard runs down to other vineyards.
steps.whatsHappening: Since it already quoted בן סירא, the גמרא finishes his words. They describe how even the poor man's nights are bad and how the world seems to work against him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His house is lowest, so everyone's rainwater runs onto his roof. His vineyard is highest, so the rain washes his good soil down to other people's vineyards. Both of his properties sit in the worst spot.

phrases.english: Ben Sira says:
"Even the nights [are bad].
His roof is at the lowest of the roofs,
and his vineyard is at the top of the mountains,
[so] the rain from the roofs [runs] to his roof,
and the soil of his vineyard [washes] to the vineyards."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the בן סירא passage begun in Step 8.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even the nights of the poor are bad. His house and his vineyard are both in the worst position.

steps.title: Anyone may force a move up to ארץ ישראל or ירושלים
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה rules that anyone may force the family to move to ארץ ישראל or ירושלים, but no one may force them to leave. This applies to men and women alike.
steps.simpleTranslation: Everyone can make the family move up to ארץ ישראל, but no one can make them leave. Everyone can make the family move up to ירושלים, but no one can make them leave. This is true for both men and women.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It rules that a husband or wife can force the family to move to ארץ ישראל or ירושלים, but cannot force them to move away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier משנה said a spouse usually cannot force a move. This משנה gives the exception: moving up in holiness to ארץ ישראל or ירושלים can be forced. Moving away cannot.

keyTerms.meaning: Short for מתניתין, 'our משנה'. It marks the start of a new משנה.
Bring up. Here it means forcing the family to move up to a holier place.
Take out. Here it means forcing the family to leave.
Both men and women. Either spouse has this power.

steps.confusionAlert: 'וְאֵין הַכֹּל מוֹצִיאִין' does not mean 'some can take out and some cannot.' It means no one can force the family to leave.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the basis for the halacha that a spouse who wants to move to ארץ ישראל can insist on it.

phrases.english: MISHNA:
All may bring [their family] up to Eretz Yisrael,
phrases.notes: This means a family member can force the household to move up to ארץ ישראל.

phrases.english: but not all may take [them] out.
All may bring [their family] up to Jerusalem,
but not all may take [them] out.
Both men and women [have this right].

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new משנה about forcing a move.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Either spouse may force a move to ארץ ישראל or ירושלים, but not a move away from them.

steps.title: Which currency pays the כתובה: the תנא קמא's cases
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that in three cases the כתובה is paid in the currency of ארץ ישראל: when the couple married and divorced there, married there and divorced in קפוטקיא, or married in קפוטקיא and divorced there.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he married her in ארץ ישראל and divorced her in ארץ ישראל, he pays her in ארץ ישראל money. If he married her in ארץ ישראל and divorced her in קפוטקיא, he pays her in ארץ ישראל money. If he married her in קפוטקיא and divorced her in ארץ ישראל, he pays her in ארץ ישראל money.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה moves to a new topic: which country's coins are used to pay the כתובה when the marriage and divorce happen in different places. The תנא קמא says that whenever ארץ ישראל is involved, he pays in ארץ ישראל money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The coins of קפוטקיא were worth more than the coins of ארץ ישראל. In the תנא קמא's view, if either the wedding or the divorce happened in ארץ ישראל, the husband pays with the cheaper ארץ ישראל coins.

keyTerms.meaning: Cappadocia, a region outside ארץ ישראל whose coins were worth more.

phrases.english: If he married a woman in Eretz Yisrael
and divorced her in Eretz Yisrael,
he gives her [the כתובה] in the money of Eretz Yisrael.
If he married a woman in Eretz Yisrael
and divorced her in Cappadocia,
he gives her the money of Eretz Yisrael.
If he married a woman in Cappadocia
and divorced her in Eretz Yisrael,
he gives her the money of Eretz Yisrael.

steps.triggerLanguage: נָשָׂא אִשָּׁה בְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל וְגֵרְשָׁהּ בְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The משנה moves on to a new topic: the currency of the כתובה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to the תנא קמא, whenever either the marriage or the divorce took place in ארץ ישראל, the כתובה is paid in ארץ ישראל currency.

steps.title: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל disagrees, and the case everyone agrees on
steps.stepSummary: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל holds that if they married in קפוטקיא and divorced in ארץ ישראל, he pays in קפוטקיא money. Everyone agrees that if both happened in קפוטקיא, he pays in קפוטקיא money.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: He pays her in קפוטקיא money. If he married her in קפוטקיא and divorced her in קפוטקיא, he pays her in קפוטקיא money.
steps.whatsHappening: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל disagrees about the last case. If the wedding was in קפוטקיא, he pays with קפוטקיא coins. Then the משנה gives the simple case where everything happened in קפוטקיא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, the place of the wedding decides the currency, even if the divorce was in ארץ ישראל. When both the wedding and the divorce were in קפוטקיא, there is no argument: he pays in קפוטקיא money.

keyTerms.meaning: Says. It introduces a different opinion.

steps.whatToRemember: The תנא קמא pays in ארץ ישראל money whenever ארץ ישראל is involved. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל follows the place of the wedding. Both agree that if everything happened in קפוטקיא, he pays in קפוטקיא money.
steps.confusionAlert: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל is arguing only about the case right before his words: married in קפוטקיא and divorced in ארץ ישראל. He does not argue about the other cases.

phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
He gives her the money of Cappadocia.
If he married a woman in Cappadocia
and divorced her in Cappadocia,
he gives her the money of Cappadocia.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר: נוֹתֵן לָהּ מִמְּעוֹת קַפּוֹטְקְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a dissenting view on the last case of Step 13, then the case everyone agrees on.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל: the currency follows the place of the wedding. Everyone agrees: married and divorced in קפוטקיא means payment in קפוטקיא money.

steps.title: What does 'all can force the move up' add?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins discussing the משנה and asks what the word 'all' in 'all can force the family to go up' comes to include.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: The משנה said 'All can force the family to go up.' What does the word 'all' come to include?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens its discussion of the משנה from Step 12. It asks what extra case the word 'all' adds, which sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה could have just said 'one can force the family to move up.' Adding 'all' sounds like it is meant to include someone we might have left out. The גמרא wants to know who that is.

keyTerms.meaning: To include; to bring in an extra case
Can force to go up (move to ארץ ישראל)

phrases.english: Gemara: 'All can force to go up'
comes to include what?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts the גמרא's discussion of the משנה quoted in Step 12.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which extra case the word 'all' in 'all can force to go up' comes to include.

steps.title: It includes slaves
steps.stepSummary: The word 'all' includes slaves. They too can be forced to move to ארץ ישראל with the household.
steps.simpleTranslation: It comes to include slaves.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that 'all' comes to include slaves.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without the extra word, we might think the rule only covers family members like a husband or wife. 'All' widens it so the household's slaves can also be made to move to ארץ ישראל.

phrases.english: It comes to include slaves.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 15.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The word 'all' includes slaves in the rule of being forced to move to ארץ ישראל.

steps.title: What if the משנה already mentions slaves?
steps.stepSummary: Some versions of the משנה openly list slaves. According to those versions, the גמרא asks what 'all' comes to add.
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to the one whose version of the משנה openly mentions slaves, what does 'all' come to include?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that some versions of the משנה already say 'slaves' outright, so the answer in Step 16 would not work for them. It asks again what 'all' adds, setting up a new answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If slaves are written openly in the משנה, they cannot also be the extra case hidden in the word 'all.' So for that version, 'all' must be adding something else.

keyTerms.meaning: According to the one who teaches (whose version reads)

phrases.english: And according to the one who teaches slaves openly,
phrases.notes: Some versions of the משנה say the rule applies to men, women and slaves, so slaves are already written there.

phrases.english: it comes to include what?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּלְמַאן דְּתָנֵי עֲבָדִים בְּהֶדְיָא לְאֵתוֹיֵי מַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that Step 16's answer fails for another version of the משנה and asks again.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What 'all' adds according to the version of the משנה that already lists slaves.

steps.title: It includes moving from a nice home to a worse one
steps.stepSummary: The word 'all' teaches that a person can force the family to move to ארץ ישראל even if they leave a nice home and get a worse one.
steps.simpleTranslation: It comes to include moving from a nice home to a bad home.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that 'all' means the family can be forced to move to ארץ ישראל even when the new home is worse than the old one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We might think a person can only force the move if living conditions stay the same or get better. 'All' teaches that moving to ארץ ישראל is so important that even a downgrade in housing does not stop it.

keyTerms.meaning: A home or place to live

steps.whatToRemember: Moving to ארץ ישראל can be required even if it means a worse home than the one you had outside it.

phrases.english: It comes to include from a nice home
phrases.notes: He means a nice home outside ארץ ישראל.

phrases.english: to a bad home.
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the ה in round brackets, so the word is read as הרע.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 17's question for the version that already lists slaves.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'All' includes forcing a move to ארץ ישראל even from a nice home to a worse one.

steps.title: What does 'all may not force them out' add?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא turns to the next line of the משנה, 'and all may not force them out,' and asks what 'all' comes to include there.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said 'And all may not force them out.' What does this come to include?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the second half of the משנה's rule and asks the same kind of question. This sets up the next answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says no one may force a person to leave ארץ ישראל. The word 'all' again sounds extra, so the גמרא looks for the special case it covers.

keyTerms.meaning: Can force to go out (leave ארץ ישראל)

phrases.english: 'And all may not force out'
comes to include what?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the first half of the משנה's rule to the second half.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which extra case 'all may not force them out' comes to include.

steps.title: A runaway slave who reached ארץ ישראל
steps.stepSummary: It includes a slave who ran away from outside ארץ ישראל into ארץ ישראל. The master must sell him there and may not take him back out, because of the מצוה of settling ארץ ישראל.
steps.simpleTranslation: It comes to include a slave who ran away from outside ארץ ישראל to ארץ ישראל. We tell the master: Sell him here and then go, because of the מצוה of settling ארץ ישראל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that even a runaway slave who reached ארץ ישראל cannot be forced back out by his master. The master has to sell him in ארץ ישראל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally an owner can bring back his runaway slave. Here the slave has reached ארץ ישראל, so taking him out would undo the מצוה of living there. The fix is that the master sells him in ארץ ישראל and leaves without him.

keyTerms.meaning: The מצוה of settling ארץ ישראל

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that the מצוה of settling ארץ ישראל is strong enough to limit an owner's normal rights over his own slave.

phrases.english: It comes to include a slave who ran away
from outside the Land to the Land,
for we say to him:
phrases.notes: 'Him' is the master who came to get his slave back.

phrases.english: Sell him here and go,
because of the settling of ארץ ישראל.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 19.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'All may not force out' includes a runaway slave who reached ארץ ישראל. His master must sell him there and may not take him out.

steps.title: What does 'all can force the move to ירושלים' add?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what 'all' adds in the משנה's line 'all can force the family to go up to ירושלים.'
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said 'All can force the family to go up to ירושלים.' What does this come to include?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now asks the same question about the משנה's rule for ירושלים. This sets up the final answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה gives a second level: inside ארץ ישראל, one can force a move to ירושלים. The גמרא wants to know what the word 'all' adds here too.

keyTerms.meaning: Can force to go up to ירושלים
It comes to include what? The standard question about an extra word

phrases.english: 'All can force to go up to ירושלים'
comes to include what?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the משנה's rule about ירושלים.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which extra case 'all can force to go up to ירושלים' comes to include.

steps.title: Moving to a worse home in ירושלים
steps.stepSummary: 'All' teaches that the family can be forced to move from a nice home elsewhere in ארץ ישראל to a worse home in ירושלים.
steps.simpleTranslation: It comes to include moving from a nice home to a bad home.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the same answer as in Step 18, now applied to ירושלים. One can force a move to ירושלים even if the new home there is worse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just as moving to ארץ ישראל is worth a worse home, moving to ירושלים is worth it too. The words are the same as Step 18, but now the move is from elsewhere in ארץ ישראל to ירושלים.

keyTerms.meaning: From a nice home to a bad home (here, inside ארץ ישראל)
The bad one. The text is printed both ways

steps.whatToRemember: Both moving to ארץ ישראל and moving to ירושלים can be forced, even when the new home is worse than the old one.
steps.confusionAlert: Step 18 and this step use the same words, but they are about different moves. Step 18 is a move from outside ארץ ישראל into ארץ ישראל. Here the move is from another place in ארץ ישראל into ירושלים.

phrases.english: It comes to include from a nice home
phrases.notes: Here he means a nice home somewhere else in ארץ ישראל.

phrases.english: to a bad home.
phrases.notes: He means a worse home in ירושלים.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 21 with the same idea as Step 18, now applied to ירושלים.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'All' includes forcing a move to ירושלים even from a nice home elsewhere to a worse home in ירושלים.

steps.title: What does 'all' add in 'all may not take out'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the word 'all' adds in the משנה's line that a person may not force the family out of ירושלים.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said 'and all may not take out.' What does the word 'all' come to include?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא keeps going through the משנה phrase by phrase. Now it asks what 'all' adds in the line about not taking the family out of ירושלים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 22 explained the 'all' in 'all can force the family to go up to ירושלים.' This step asks the same question about the second half of that line, which says nobody may force them out of ירושלים.

keyTerms.meaning: take out, force someone to move away
to include, to add a case

phrases.english: "And all may not take out"
phrases.notes: This is the line about ירושלים: nobody may force the family to leave it.

phrases.english: comes to include what?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the first half of the ירושלים line ('all can force up') to its second half ('all may not take out').
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What extra case is included by the word 'all' in 'all may not take out' of ירושלים?

steps.title: Even a move from a bad home to a nice home
steps.stepSummary: 'All' teaches that you may not force the family out of ירושלים even if they would leave a bad home there for a nice home somewhere else.
steps.simpleTranslation: It comes to include even a move from a bad home to a nice home.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers: you cannot force the family out of ירושלים even when the new home would be better.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You might have thought that moving someone to a nicer place is allowed, since it helps them. 'All' teaches that living in ירושלים matters more than how nice the house is, so they still cannot be forced to leave.
steps.whatToRemember: Going up: you can force the family to move to a worse home in ירושלים. Leaving: you cannot force them out of ירושלים, even to a better home.

phrases.english: to include even
from a bad home to a nice home.
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the ה in round brackets, so read it as הָרַע. The bad home is in ירושלים and the nice one is outside it.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְאֵתוֹיֵי אֲפִילּוּ מִנָּוֶה הָרַע לְנָוֶה הַיָּפֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 23.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The family may not be forced out of ירושלים even when they would move from a bad home there to a nice home outside it.

steps.title: Why the משנה repeats 'may not take out'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that the second 'may not take out' was written mainly to match the wording of the first part of the משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since the first part of the משנה said 'may not take out,' the last part also said 'may not take out.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the משנה's style. The phrase 'may not take out' appears in the ירושלים line because the same phrase was used in the ארץ ישראל line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule about not taking a family out of ירושלים did not really need its own words, because it could have been learned from the first part. The תנא repeated the phrase so that both parts would have the same pattern.

keyTerms.meaning: the first part of a משנה
the last part of a משנה

steps.confusionAlert: This step does not take back the rule from step 24. It only explains why the משנה used the same wording in both parts.

phrases.english: And since he taught in the first part "may not take out,"
phrases.notes: The first part is the line about ארץ ישראל: nobody may force the family out of the land.

phrases.english: he also taught in the last part "may not take out."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a note on the משנה's wording after explaining what it includes.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: One might ask why the ירושלים line needs its own 'may not take out' if the rule could be learned from the first part.
steps.terutzMaskana: It was written to keep the same pattern as the ארץ ישראל line.

steps.title: A ברייתא: one spouse wants to move up to ארץ ישראל
steps.stepSummary: Whichever spouse wants to move up to ארץ ישראל can force the other. If the wife refuses, she leaves without a כתובה. If the husband refuses, he must divorce her and pay the כתובה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: If he says to go up and she says not to go up, we force her to go up. If she won't, she is divorced without a כתובה. If she says to go up and he says not to go up, we force him to go up. If he won't, he must divorce her and give her the כתובה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that spells out what happens when a husband and wife disagree about moving to ארץ ישראל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wanting to go up to ארץ ישראל always wins, whether it is the husband or the wife who wants it. The spouse who refuses pays the price. A wife who refuses loses her כתובה, and a husband who refuses must divorce her and pay it.

keyTerms.meaning: to go up (move to ארץ ישראל)
the marriage contract and the money it promises the wife

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught: If he says to go up,
and she says not to go up —
we force her to go up,
and if not — she leaves without a כתובה.
If she says to go up,
and he says not to go up —
we force him to go up,
and if not — he must divorce her and give the כתובה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא that fills in the details behind the משנה's rule that anyone can force the family to go up to ארץ ישראל.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The spouse who wants to move to ארץ ישראל can force the other. A refusing wife loses her כתובה, and a refusing husband must divorce her and pay it.

steps.title: The ברייתא continues: one spouse wants to leave ארץ ישראל
steps.stepSummary: Whichever spouse wants to stay in ארץ ישראל can stop the other from leaving. A wife who insists on leaving loses her כתובה. A husband who insists on leaving must divorce her and pay it.
steps.simpleTranslation: If she says to leave and he says not to leave, we force her not to leave. If she won't stay, she is divorced without a כתובה. If he says to leave and she says not to leave, we force him not to leave. If he won't stay, he must divorce her and give her the כתובה.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא now covers the opposite case: a couple living in ארץ ישראל where one spouse wants to leave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This works just like the moving-up case. Staying in ארץ ישראל always wins. The spouse who insists on leaving is the one who loses: the wife loses her כתובה, or the husband has to divorce her and pay it.

keyTerms.meaning: he must divorce her (literally, send her out)

steps.whatToRemember: Whether moving up or staying, the spouse who chooses ארץ ישראל always wins. If the other spouse refuses, that refusing spouse loses: a wife loses her כתובה, and a husband must divorce and pay it.
steps.confusionAlert: Watch the two meanings of 'leave': לָצֵאת means leaving ארץ ישראל, while תֵּצֵא and יוֹצִיא mean leaving the marriage through divorce.

phrases.english: If she says to leave,
and he says not to leave —
we force her not to leave,
and if not — she leaves without a כתובה.
If he says to leave,
and she says not to leave —
we force him not to leave,
and if not — he must divorce her and give the כתובה.

steps.triggerLanguage: הִיא אוֹמֶרֶת לָצֵאת, וְהוּא אוֹמֵר שֶׁלֹּא לָצֵאת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Second half of the same ברייתא: the case of leaving instead of going up.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The spouse who wants to stay in ארץ ישראל can stop the other from leaving. If the other spouse still refuses to stay, that spouse loses: a wife loses her כתובה, and a husband must divorce and pay it.

steps.title: The next line of the משנה contradicts itself
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא turns to the משנה's line about marrying in one place and divorcing in another, and announces that the line contradicts itself.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'If one married a woman, etc.' This line itself is difficult.
steps.whatsHappening: This step sets up the next discussion. The גמרא quotes the start of the next line of the משנה and says it has a problem inside it. The details come in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: That משנה line deals with someone who married in ארץ ישראל and divorced in קפוטקיא, or the other way around, and says which currency the כתובה is paid in. 'הא גופה קשיא' means the line's own rulings seem to clash with each other. The גמרא is not bringing an outside source here.

keyTerms.meaning: this itself is difficult (it contradicts itself)

phrases.english: "If one married a woman," etc.
This itself is difficult:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the topic of moving and begins a new section of the משנה about the currency of the כתובה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's rulings on paying the כתובה when the marriage and divorce took place in different lands.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Internal contradiction: the parts of that משנה line seem to clash with each other. The details are given in the next step.

steps.title: The first and last cases of the משנה seem to follow opposite rules
steps.stepSummary: The first case suggests we follow the place of the obligation, while the last case suggests we follow the place of collection.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה teaches: if a man married a woman in ארץ ישראל and divorced her in קפוטקיא, he pays her in the money of ארץ ישראל. That suggests we follow the place where the obligation began. But the last case says: if he married her in קפוטקיא and divorced her in ארץ ישראל, he also pays in the money of ארץ ישראל. That suggests we follow the place where the money is collected!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now spells out the contradiction it announced in step 28. It sets the two cases side by side to show they point in opposite directions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first case, the money matches the place of the wedding, where the obligation began. In the second case, the money matches the place of the divorce, where she collects. One משנה cannot seem to hold both rules, unless something else explains why ארץ ישראל money wins both times.

keyTerms.meaning: Cappadocia, a place outside ארץ ישראל
The obligation, or lien: the place where the debt started
Collection: the place where the money is actually paid
Now look at the last part

steps.confusionAlert: Both cases end with the same answer (money of ארץ ישראל). The contradiction is not in the answer. It is in the reason each answer seems to be based on.

phrases.english: It teaches: if one married a woman in Eretz Yisrael
and divorced her in Cappadocia,
he gives her from the money of Eretz Yisrael
so apparently we go after the place of the obligation.
phrases.notes: The obligation started at the wedding, so this means we follow the place of the wedding.

phrases.english: Now say the last part:
if one married a woman in Cappadocia
and divorced her in Eretz Yisrael,
he gives her from the money of Eretz Yisrael
so apparently we go after the place of collection!

steps.triggerLanguage: אַלְמָא בָּתַר שִׁיעְבּוּדָא אָזְלִינַן. אֵימָא סֵיפָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Fills in the contradiction that step 28 announced
steps.kashyaTarget: The two cases of the משנה about marrying in one place and divorcing in another
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The רישא implies we follow the place of the obligation. The סיפא implies we follow the place of collection. The two implied rules contradict each other.

steps.title: רבה: The משנה is giving a leniency for a כתובה
steps.stepSummary: רבה explains that the תנא always lets the husband pay in the cheaper money because he holds a כתובה is only דרבנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: Here they taught one of the leniencies of a כתובה. The תנא holds that a כתובה is a rabbinic obligation.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה answers the contradiction. Neither case follows a fixed rule about place. Both cases simply give the husband the easier way out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the money of ארץ ישראל was worth less, the husband pays with it whether the wedding or the divorce happened there. This leniency makes sense because the תנא holds the כתובה is only דרבנן, and a rabbinic debt can be paid in the easier way.

keyTerms.meaning: One of the leniencies of a כתובה
A rabbinic law, not from the תורה

steps.whyThisMatters: This links a money question to a basic dispute about where the כתובה comes from: the רבנן or the תורה.

phrases.english: Rabba said:
They taught here one of the leniencies of a ketubah.
He holds that a ketubah is rabbinic.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה: מִקּוּלֵּי כְתוּבָּה שָׁנוּ כָּאן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction from step 29
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reframing: both cases follow one principle of leniency, not two rules about place
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה seemed to switch between following the place of the obligation and the place of collection
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה always picks the cheaper money as a leniency, because it holds a כתובה is דרבנן

steps.title: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל holds a כתובה is from the תורה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that רבן שמעון בן גמליאל requires payment in the money of קפוטקיא because he holds a כתובה is דאורייתא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: he pays her in the money of קפוטקיא. He holds that a כתובה is a Torah obligation.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the other opinion in the משנה and explains the reason behind it. This is the other side of רבה's explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a כתובה is דאורייתא, there is no room for a leniency. So we follow the place where the obligation began, the wedding in קפוטקיא, and she gets the more valuable money.
steps.whatToRemember: The dispute: the first תנא holds כתובה is דרבנן, so the husband pays in the cheaper money. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל holds it is דאורייתא, so we follow the place of the wedding.

phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
he gives her from the money of Cappadocia.
He holds that a ketubah is from the Torah.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר: נוֹתֵן לָהּ מִמְּעוֹת קַפּוֹטְקְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reason for the opposing opinion, matching רבה's explanation of the first תנא
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the root of the dispute
steps.terutzHavaAmina: It was unclear why רבן שמעון בן גמליאל disagrees with the first תנא
steps.terutzMaskana: He holds a כתובה is דאורייתא, so no leniency applies and we follow the place of the obligation

steps.title: A ברייתא: which money pays a loan document
steps.stepSummary: A loan document is paid in the money of the place written in it. If no place is written, it is paid in the money of the place where it is brought to court.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: if someone brings a loan document against another person, and it says בבל, it is paid with the money of בבל. If it says ארץ ישראל, it is paid with the money of ארץ ישראל. If no place is written, and he brings it in בבל, it is paid with the money of בבל. If he brings it in ארץ ישראל, it is paid with the money of ארץ ישראל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא about a regular שטר חוב. It sets the general rules for which money pays a debt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the document names a place, we follow that place. If it names no place, we follow the place where the lender produces it for collection.

keyTerms.meaning: He collects it (he pays it with)

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
one who produces a loan document against his fellow,
if Babylonia is written in it,
he pays it with the money of Babylonia;
if Eretz Yisrael is written in it,
he pays it with the money of Eretz Yisrael.
If it is written without a place:
if he produced it in Babylonia,
he pays it with the money of Babylonia;
if he produced it in Eretz Yisrael,
he pays it with the money of Eretz Yisrael.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: הַמּוֹצִיא שְׁטַר חוֹב עַל חֲבֵירוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the כתובה to the related rules for a regular loan document
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Pay in the money of the place written in the שטר. If none is written, pay in the money of the place where it is produced.

steps.title: "Money" with no coin named: the borrower chooses; a כתובה is different
steps.stepSummary: If the document just says "money," the borrower may pay with any coin he wants. The ברייתא closes by saying that a כתובה is different.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the document just says "money" without naming a coin, the borrower pays with whatever he wants. This is not so with a כתובה.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא ends with one more rule for loans. Then it points out that this rule does not work the same way for a כתובה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With an unclear loan document, the borrower gets the benefit of the doubt and can pay with any coin. The ברייתא then says a כתובה is different, but it does not say which of its rules it means. Step 34 asks this, and step 35 answers that it goes back to the first rule, about the place written in the document.
steps.whatToRemember: With a regular loan, an unclear document lets the borrower choose the coin. The ברייתא adds that a כתובה is different. Step 35 explains which rule that refers to.

phrases.english: If it says just "money," without naming a coin,
the borrower pays it with whatever he wants.
This is not so with a ketubah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the ברייתא and sets a כתובה apart from a regular loan
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If a loan document says only "money," the borrower chooses the coin. The ברייתא adds that a כתובה is different, and step 35 shows this refers to the first clause.

steps.title: Which clause does 'but not a כתובה' refer to?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which part of the ברייתא the closing words 'this does not apply to a כתובה' are attached to.
steps.simpleTranslation: To which part of the ברייתא does this refer?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short question: the ברייתא ended by saying 'but not so for a כתובה'. Which rule in the ברייתא was it talking about?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא had several clauses: the place written in the document, no place written, and plain 'money'. The words 'not a כתובה' could go back to any of them, so the גמרא needs to know which one is being limited.

keyTerms.meaning: On which one? To which clause does this refer?

phrases.english: To which [clause does this refer]?
phrases.notes: He is asking about the ברייתא's closing words from step 33: 'this does not apply to a כתובה.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks where the limit stated at the end of step 33 belongs.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which clause of the ברייתא is limited by the words 'but not a כתובה'.

steps.title: It refers to the first clause, unlike רבן שמעון בן גמליאל
steps.stepSummary: רב משרשיא says it goes back to the first clause. The rule of always paying in the money of the place written in the document does not hold for a כתובה. This disagrees with רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, who holds a כתובה is דאורייתא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב משרשיא said: It refers to the first clause. It comes to exclude the view of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, who said that a כתובה is from the Torah.
steps.whatsHappening: רב משרשיא answers that 'not a כתובה' goes back to the first rule: a loan document is paid in the money of the place written in it. For a כתובה, that rule does not always apply.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A loan is always paid in the money of the place written in the document, whether that money is cheaper or more expensive. For a כתובה, the תנא holds it is only דרבנן, so the husband pays in the cheaper money, as רבה explained in step 30. This argues with רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, who holds a כתובה is דאורייתא and must be paid strictly, as in step 31.

keyTerms.meaning: The first clause of a משנה or ברייתא
To exclude, meaning to reject another opinion
The marriage contract that promises the wife money

steps.whatToRemember: A loan document is always paid in the money of its written place. A כתובה is different, because this תנא holds it is only דרבנן, unlike רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.

phrases.english: Rav Mesharshiya said: [It refers] to the first clause,
phrases.notes: The first clause is the rule from step 32: a loan document is paid in the money of the place written in it.

phrases.english: to exclude [the view] of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel,
who said a marriage contract is from the Torah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 34.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The limit refers to the first clause. The rule of always following the place written in the document does not apply to a כתובה, rejecting רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.

steps.title: Maybe 'money' means pieces of raw silver
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the ruling that if the document just says 'כסף', the borrower may pay with any coin. It then asks: maybe 'כסף' means silver strips, not coins.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the document says just 'money', the borrower may pay with whatever he wants. But say it means silver strips!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the ruling from step 33 again in order to question it. The word כסף can mean 'money' or 'silver', so maybe the lender is owed raw silver and not coins.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If כסף means raw silver strips, the borrower could not simply pay with any coin he likes. The challenge asks how the ברייתא knows the document means coins at all.

keyTerms.meaning: A strip or bar of raw silver, not a coin
'But say...', which offers another way to read the case

phrases.english: If it says in it 'money' without details —
phrases.notes: The word כסף means both 'money' and 'silver.' That double meaning is what the question is built on.

phrases.english: the borrower may pay it with whatever he wants.
But say [it means] silver strips?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the 'plain money' clause from step 33 and questions how that case is defined.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that 'כסף' with no details may be paid with any coin.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: כסף can mean raw silver, so maybe the document requires silver strips and not just any coin.

steps.title: The document says 'coins'
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר explains that the ברייתא is talking about a document that writes 'coins' without saying which ones.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר said: It is a case where 'coin' is written in it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר answers that the document clearly says 'coins'. The only thing missing is which kind of coin.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the document says 'coins', raw silver strips are ruled out. The leniency is only about which coin the borrower may use.

keyTerms.meaning: Where it is written in it

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar said:
[It is a case] where 'coin' is written in it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר: דִּכְתִיב בֵּיהּ מַטְבֵּעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 36.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: כסף could mean raw silver strips.
steps.terutzMaskana: The document says 'coins', so only the type of coin is left open.

steps.title: Maybe small coins are meant
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if it just says 'silver coins', maybe the borrower may pay with tiny small-value coins.
steps.simpleTranslation: But say it means small coins!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes further. If the document says 'coins' without saying which kind, maybe the borrower can pay with the smallest coins there are.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If פריטי count, the borrower could give back far less than was meant. The challenge asks what sets the lowest value of a 'silver coin'.

phrases.english: But say [it means] small coins?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי אלעזר's answer from step 37.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אלעזר's case of a document that says 'coins'.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'Coins' could include the smallest coins, which would let the borrower pay very little.

steps.title: Nobody makes small coins out of silver
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא answers that people do not make small coins of silver, so a 'silver coin' must mean a coin of real value.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: People do not make small coins out of silver.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא explains that small coins are never made of silver. So a document that speaks of silver coins cannot mean tiny coins.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer uses how people really act: silver is used only for larger coins. So the borrower may choose which silver coin to pay with, but not drop down to tiny coins.

keyTerms.meaning: People do not do this; it is not normal practice

steps.whatToRemember: With 'plain money', the borrower picks any real silver coin. Not raw silver, and not tiny small coins.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
People do not make small coins of silver.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: פְּרִיטֵי דְכַסְפָּא לָא עָבְדִי אִינָשֵׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 38.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Appeal to how people normally act
steps.terutzMaskana: Silver is not used for small coins, so the coin must be one of real value.

steps.title: Always live in ארץ ישראל
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that a person should live in ארץ ישראל even in a city that is mostly non-Jewish, and not outside the land even in a city that is mostly Jewish. Living in the land is like having a God, as the פסוק says.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: A person should always live in ארץ ישראל, even in a city mostly of non-Jews, and not outside the land, even in a city mostly of Jews. Whoever lives in ארץ ישראל is like one who has a God, and whoever lives outside is like one who has no God, as it says: 'To give you the land of כנען, to be your God.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic connected to the משנה's discussion of living in ארץ ישראל. It brings a ברייתא that strongly praises living in the land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא ranks the land above the Jewish makeup of one's city: a mostly non-Jewish city in the land beats a mostly Jewish city outside it. Its proof is a פסוק that links being given the land with having ה׳ as your God.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
A person should always live in the Land of Israel
even in a city that is mostly non-Jews,
and he should not live outside the Land
even in a city that is mostly Jews,
because anyone who lives in the Land of Israel
is like one who has a God,
and anyone who lives outside the Land
is like one who has no God.
As it says: 'To give you the land of Canaan,'
phrases.notes: ויקרא 25:38

phrases.english: 'to be your God.'

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: לְעוֹלָם יָדוּר אָדָם בְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the topic of currency and opens a new section on living in ארץ ישראל.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One should always live in ארץ ישראל, even among non-Jews, and not outside it, even among Jews. Living in the land is like having a God.

steps.title: Does someone outside the land really have no God?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא is surprised: can it be that anyone who lives outside the land has no God?
steps.simpleTranslation: And does anyone who doesn't live in the land have no God?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the ברייתא's strong words. It cannot mean that a Jew living outside the land literally has no God.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Read literally, the ברייתא would say ה׳ is not the God of Jews outside the land, which cannot be right. So the words must mean something else.
steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not doubting that living in ארץ ישראל matters. It only questions the literal words 'has no God'.

phrases.english: And anyone who does not live in the Land
has no God?!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֹל שֶׁאֵינוֹ דָּר בָּאָרֶץ אֵין לוֹ אֱלוֹהַּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the wording of the ברייתא in step 40.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's phrase 'like one who has no God'.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Taken literally, it would deny that a Jew outside the land has God, which is impossible.

steps.title: It means it is as if he serves עבודה זרה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains the ברייתא's meaning: living outside the land is considered as if one serves עבודה זרה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it comes to tell you: anyone who lives outside the land is as if he serves idols.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reinterprets the strong words. They are a comparison, not a literal statement.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'as if' shows this is a comparison about how serious it is to live outside the land. The person still has God, but leaving the land is treated very seriously.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, this comes to tell you

phrases.english: Rather, [this is] to tell you:
anyone who lives outside the Land
is as if he worships idols.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 41.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא literally says he has no God.
steps.terutzMaskana: It means living outside the land is as if he serves עבודה זרה.

steps.title: Support from דוד's words
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a פסוק where דוד says that being driven out of ה׳'s inheritance is like being told to go serve other gods.
steps.simpleTranslation: And so it says about דוד: 'For they have driven me out today from attaching myself to the inheritance of ה׳, saying: Go, serve other gods.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a פסוק to support the idea that leaving the land is compared to עבודה זרה. In it, דוד speaks about being chased out of the land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: דוד was forced to flee from שאול out of the land. He describes this as being told 'go serve other gods', which links leaving the land to עבודה זרה.

keyTerms.meaning: And so it says about דוד
The inheritance of ה׳, meaning ארץ ישראל

phrases.english: And so it says about David:
'For they have driven me out today'
phrases.notes: שמואל א 26:19

phrases.english: 'from attaching myself to the inheritance of the Lord,'
'saying: Go, serve other gods.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a פסוק to support the explanation in step 42.
steps.raayaObject: Living outside the land is compared to serving עבודה זרה.
steps.raayaSupportSource: שמואל א 26:19, where דוד speaks of being driven from ה׳'s inheritance.

steps.title: Who ever told דוד to serve idols?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: nobody actually told דוד to serve other gods, so what does the פסוק mean?
steps.simpleTranslation: But who said to דוד, 'Go, serve other gods'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that no one really told דוד to serve idols. This sets up the explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the words cannot be literal, the פסוק must be describing what being sent out of the land amounts to. This question is what turns the פסוק into a proof.

phrases.english: But who said to David:
'Go, serve other gods'?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי מִי אָמַר לוֹ לְדָוִד לֵךְ עֲבוֹד אֱלֹהִים אֲחֵרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the literal meaning of the פסוק in step 43 in order to draw out the lesson.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the פסוק means, since no one literally told דוד to serve idols.

steps.title: Living outside the land is as if serving עבודה זרה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that the פסוק teaches that anyone who lives outside the land is as if he serves עבודה זרה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it comes to tell you: anyone who lives outside the land is as if he serves idols.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question and wraps up the proof. The פסוק is teaching how serious it is to live outside ארץ ישראל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Being pushed out of the land was described by דוד as being told to serve other gods. This confirms the explanation of the ברייתא given in step 42.
steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא's 'like one who has no God' means: living outside ארץ ישראל is as if one serves עבודה זרה. The פסוק about דוד proves it.

phrases.english: Rather, [this is] to tell you:
anyone who lives outside the Land —
is as if he worships idols.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא לוֹמַר לָךְ: כׇּל הַדָּר בְּחוּצָה לָאָרֶץ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 44 and completes the proof for step 42.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Living outside ארץ ישראל is considered as if one serves עבודה זרה, as shown by דוד's words.

steps.title: רבי זירא avoids his teacher because he wants to move to ארץ ישראל
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tells that רבי זירא kept out of רב יהודה's sight, because he wanted to move to ארץ ישראל.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא was avoiding רב יהודה, because he wanted to go up to ארץ ישראל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a story about רבי זירא, who stayed away from his teacher רב יהודה because he planned to move to ארץ ישראל. This sets up the next step, which explains why he was hiding.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The steps before this one praised living in ארץ ישראל. Now we meet a student who wants to move there, but he has to avoid his own teacher. The story hints that רב יהודה is against the move. The next line tells us why.

keyTerms.meaning: to go up (to move to ארץ ישראל)

phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira was avoiding
Rav Yehuda (his teacher),
because he wanted to go up to Eretz Yisrael,

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי זֵירָא הֲוָה קָמִשְׁתְּמִיט מִינֵּיהּ דְּרַב יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the praise of living in ארץ ישראל, the גמרא brings a story where a teacher opposes moving there.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי זירא avoided רב יהודה because he planned to move to ארץ ישראל.

steps.title: רב יהודה: going up from בבל to ארץ ישראל breaks a positive מצוה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains the hiding. רב יהודה ruled that anyone who goes up from בבל to ארץ ישראל breaks a מצות עשה. It then introduces a פסוק as his source.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because רב יהודה said: Anyone who goes up from בבל to ארץ ישראל breaks a positive commandment, as it says: (the פסוק comes next).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives רב יהודה's rule, which explains why רבי זירא was hiding from him. The word "שנאמר" is setting up a פסוק that will prove the rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a surprise after all the praise of ארץ ישראל. רב יהודה does not just say moving is a bad idea. He says it breaks a real מצות עשה. His rule is only about leaving בבל, and the פסוק he relies on is about to be quoted.

keyTerms.meaning: one who goes up (moves to ארץ ישראל)
Babylonia, the big Jewish center outside ארץ ישראל
as it says (a פסוק is coming)

steps.confusionAlert: רב יהודה does not argue with the praise of ארץ ישראל in general. His rule is only about leaving בבל in particular.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up a clash between praising ארץ ישראל and a source-based reason to stay in בבל. The גמרא will need to sort this out.

phrases.english: For Rav Yehuda said:
Anyone who goes up from Babylonia to Eretz Yisrael
breaks a positive commandment, as it says:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why רבי זירא was avoiding רב יהודה in the story.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Going up from בבל to ארץ ישראל breaks a מצות עשה, and a פסוק is about to be brought as the source.
